newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Gil-Robles defends his Euro Parliament presidency.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Gil-Robles defends his Euro Parliament presidency.

text.p: Spanish conservative politician Jose Maria Gil-Robles Gil Delgado says he has an easy conscience about the backroom deal which led to his election as President of the European Parliament this week.

Gil-Robles, who will lead the assembly to its next elections in June 1999, plays down protests from smaller groups and countries in the assembly that he was undemocratically bulldozed in by the assembly's political powerhouses.
"I simply say that, if you look around to any parliament in the European Union, there's no other way of electing a president of parliament," he told Reuters in an interview.
Judging from a higher than expected protest vote for the alternative candidate France's Catherine Lalumiere, who gained almost one third of the votes on Tuesday, many deputies do not agree with him.

Under a long-standing deal between the parliament's 214-strong Socialist group and the 181-strong European People's Party (EPP), the two each preside over half of the assembly's five-year legislature.

Within the mainly Christian Democratic EPP, the choice of Gil-Robles came down to a deal between German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar. Germany and Spain are the group's two biggest national delegations.
CRUCIAL POINT IN PARLIAMENT'S HISTORY

Gil-Robles, who takes over the reins at a crucial point in the parliament's history, said the consensus between the large groups, who hold two thirds of the parliamentary seats, gave the parliament a figure who can rise above political divisions.
"In the European Parliament I think it's done in that way so that you can agree someone who is not be in the political line of one party...That's a kind of guarantee for all groups," he said.

Gil-Robles, a 61-year-old lawyer from Madrid and a member of Spain's ruling Popular Party, will lead the 626-member parliament through the closing states of the EU's crucial review of its structure and institutions -- the so-called Intergovernmental Conference -- where the parliament is demanding more powers.
As the EU's only directly-elected assembly, Gil-Robles said the parliament wants an EU which is "more democratic, transparent and much more efficient."
But many deputies say the parliament is not practising the democracy it preaches to the countries of central and eastern Europe, which are queueing to join the 15-nation bloc.

Only two political parties out of eight were involved in the presidential nomination and six countries -- Austria, Belgium, Finland, Ireland, the Netherlands and Sweden -- are not represented in the European Parliament bureau, its top decision-making body.
WOMEN'S ISSUE
The system could also be hard to sell to the EU women, some women deputies argue.
Under the same kind of backroom deal which brought in Gil-Robles, there were 14 candidates for as many posts as vice-president and only four of them were women.

When it came to the vote, France's Nicole Fontaine, also of the EPP, was the most popular candidate, receiving more votes than Gil-Robles did in bhis successful bid for the presidency. Second came another woman, French Socialist Nicole Pery.
Under the deal between Germany and Spain which brought Gil-Robles to office, Fontaine had been disqualified from running for president, raising protests from a group of 10 leading French women.
The European Parliament's first president was a woman, Simone Veil, but since then there has not been one.
Women hold around 30 percent of the seats in the assembly.
Parliamentary officials said it was unclear whether big groups, answerable to their national capitals, would agree to change the system, despite the increasing pressure to do so.

The major parties, more sensitive at home to electoral pressure over so-called Euroscepticism and unemployment, were unwilling to lessen their grip on what happens in Brussels and Strasbourg, they said.
PRESIDENT PLANS SOME CHANGES

Gil-Robles, hoping to find calm after the storm, believes the parliament can earn more powers through the image it projects to the outside world. He intends to change some of its more unfortunate ways, he said.

At the moment monthly plenary sessions in Strasbourg bring discussion on everything from draft legislation on pressure cookers and the maximum speed of tractors to Irish bogs and unidentified flying objects.
He intends to shift discussions on technical matters to specialised committees which deal with everything from agriculture to the environment.

"Now the plenaries are overcharged with many technical questions. We have too little time for political debate...My proposal is to improve the decision-making in committees on this kind of legislation," he said.
"That would allow more time in plenaries to try to put into practice a new kind of debate, a real debate."

He will inherit from his predecessor, Klaus Haensch, a German Socialist, one of the thorniest issues facing the parliament and one which harms its reputation -- unequal salaries earned by deputies from different member states and the consequent well-publicised abuse of expenses and perks.
"There's no sense at all that we have different salaries for the same work. That would not be accepted in any workshop in the EU," he said, saying an EU statute for deputies would solve the issue.
